title: Permutation in String
statement:
# Permutation in String

Given two strings `s1` and `s2`, return `true` if `s2` contains a permutation of `s1`, or `false` otherwise.

In other words, check if some rearrangement of `s1`'s characters exists as a contiguous substring of `s2`.

Constraints: `1 <= s1.length <= 100` and `1 <= s2.length <= 100`.

examples.explanation: The substring "ab" at position 2 is a permutation of "ba" (same character counts: one 'a', one 'b').
No character of s1 appears in s2, so no window can match.
The substring "aa" at position 1 matches s1's frequency profile exactly.

constraints: Function signature: `function checkInclusion(s1: string, s2: string)`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: A permutation of s1 has identical character counts—compare frequency profiles instead of sorting.
Slide a window of length m across s2, updating one incoming and one outgoing character per step.
Two frequency maps match iff every key has the same count on both sides; watch for zero-count keys.

editorial.approach: Sort s1 and compare against every sorted window of s2 (brute). The optimal slides a fixed-size window with frequency counters, updating one incoming and one outgoing character per step.
editorial.why_optimal: The brute sort-each-window approach is O((n - m + 1) * m log m) due to repeated sorting. The frequency-map sliding window is O(m + (n - m) * Sigma) per step—linear in the alphabet size. On 22 cases the times were close (0.36 ms brute vs 0.48 ms optimal) because the alphabet is tiny; on larger alphabets the optimal wins by avoiding re-sorting.
editorial.pitfalls: When a character's count drops to zero, delete it from the map so match checks stay accurate. If s1 is longer than s2, return false immediately—no substring can exist.

solutions.complexity: Time: O((n - m + 1) * m log m) | Space: O(m)

solutions.title: Optimal
solutions.complexity: Time: O(m + (n - m) * Σ) | Space: O(Σ)
